title: It Has Not Gone Out Since
logline: In lime country under a mountain wall, a pit kiln of mud and brick has been burning without a break for months: broken stone and coconut logs go in at the top in alternate layers all day and all night, burnt lime is raked out through a tunnel at the bottom, and the fire that is doing the work was started with a kerosene rag nobody there can remember lighting.
human_question: What is holding this up — the thing that started it, or the thing that arrived an hour ago?

place.what_kind_of_place: A belt of crystalline limestone and dolomite in hill country below a long mountain scarp, worked for lime for longer than anyone can date. The quarries are pits and faces in the valley floor and lower slopes, some of them more than fifteen metres deep, where stone is loosened and then broken down by hand with sledgehammers to lumps of an inch or two. The kilns are not buildings and not stacks. Each is a crucible-shaped pit, roughly a metre across at the top and a metre and a half to two metres deep, with a curved bottom, sunk inside a chamber of mud and brick, floored with a grating of steel rod that will not let unburnt stone through, and opened at the base by a short tunnel through which the burnt lime is drawn. The ones near towns carry chimneys up to twenty-five feet; the ones in the interior villages have nothing over the mouth but a roof of coconut thatch. Beside each kiln stands the fuel: coconut trunk in heavy lengths, and husk, which burns unevenly and is the crew's constant argument with the fire. The kiln is charged in alternate layers, wood and stone, wood and stone, and it is not a batch: as the charge sinks, more is thrown in on top, and the trade in this district runs kilns on a continuous process that can go for months on end. What comes out below is quicklime, sorted by hand from underburnt stone and from ash, and then slaked: water poured over a heap of it and turned with a shovel, which boils, steams and gives off heat like an argument. The district has upwards of a hundred and seventy lime concerns, more than half of them small, several thousand people in them, and an association formed to keep the small producers out of the hands of the middlemen.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because the place contains, physically, both ends of the thing this film is about. From the air at dawn it is a valley of small white smokes under a mountain wall, each smoke a kiln and each kiln a hole in the ground with a fire in it that is months old. On the ground it is two openings a few metres apart: at the top, stone and wood going in every hour of the day and night; at the bottom, a man with a long-handled hoe raking out what the fire has finished with, because nothing new can come down until what is there has gone. Those two shots, cut together, are the concept without a word spoken: help given by what keeps arriving, and help given by what gets out of the way. And the place has one violent event that only happens after everything has stopped, which is the slaking, where water and quicklime make heat and steam out of each other and the change runs one way only, for ever.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The charge, which sinks all day and is topped up all day. The colour at the kiln mouth, which is what the crew read instead of an instrument. The wind, which decides which side of the kiln draws and how hard, and which nobody can do anything about. The fuel, which is coconut trunk and husk and heats unevenly, so no two hours are the same. Rain, which stops the quarry, wets the wood and changes the burn. And the rare events, which cannot be scheduled: a kiln allowed to die for repair, a kiln relit, a draw that comes out underburnt and has to be picked over by hand.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry months, for the quarry faces, the dust and the wood, and because the burn is steadier and the smokes stand up rather than lying along the valley. The hour before first light and the hour after dark for the mouth and the glow, which are unusable in daylight. A morning of low cloud for the smokes against the mountain wall. The film wants several days rather than one, because its subject is that nothing ends: the same act at two in the afternoon and two in the morning is the whole of it.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about burning stone. A quarry face and a sledgehammer. Baskets of broken white rock. Lengths of coconut trunk stacked to head height. A hole in the ground with a fire in it that has been going since before the monsoon, fed in alternate layers by people who never see the inside of it. A hoe going into a tunnel at the bottom and quicklime coming out hot. Hands sorting good lime from underburnt stone. Water poured on a heap and the heap boiling. Smokes in a valley under a mountain at six in the morning. It has a complete shape with nothing said over it, and anyone who likes to watch difficult work done properly has a whole piece here.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same days become the sources' summary of how conditions work, which is not a claim that everything is connected but a table of who supports whom and in which direction. The summary counts six relations and names the conditions in each, and two of those relations contain exactly one mode: mind supports matter in one way only, by arising later and sustaining what was already there, and matter supports mind in one way only, by being there first. A kiln is a place where direction is not an abstraction. Stone and wood go down; lime comes out; heat goes up; nothing goes back. The voice never says the fire is a life. It says that the texts distinguish between what makes a thing happen and what keeps it happening, that the second kind of help has to arrive again within the hour, and that a thing which ceases is counted as helping by making room, in a strict sequence, which is not the same as a lesson about letting go.

sequence.on_screen: First light, high, along a valley under a long mountain wall. Small white smokes standing up out of the trees, a dozen of them, each from a shed or a roof of coconut thatch. Below them, pale quarry faces cut into the valley floor.
sequence.voice: The summary at the end of the old analysis does not say that everything is connected. It sorts the twenty-four kinds of support into six relations and counts them: mind to mind in six ways, mind to mind-and-matter in five, mind to matter in one, matter to mind in one, concept and mind and matter to mind in two, and mind-and-matter to mind-and-matter in nine [C083-M:L5; C083-P:L369–L417].

sequence.on_screen: The top of a kiln at midday. Baskets of broken white stone tipped in, then lengths of coconut trunk laid across, then stone again. The level of the charge is visibly lower than it was an hour ago, and is brought back up.
sequence.voice: One of the twenty-four is called nutriment, and it is defined as what sustains a continuity that something else began, holding it up and letting it grow [C082-P:L6843–L6850]. The text puts the hard version of it plainly: the continuity of a body's matter must keep receiving the help of the season and of food, and if that help stops the being dies [C082-P:L6866]. This fire has not been out since it was lit. It is also not the fire that was lit. It is whatever came in an hour ago.

sequence.on_screen: The bottom of the same kiln: the short tunnel, the steel grate, a long-handled hoe going in, and hot quicklime coming out into the dark. The mouth above brightens as the charge finally moves down.
sequence.voice: And one of the twenty-four is support given by not being there. In one continuity of mind, the texts say, only one moment can stand at a time, so the moment that ceases is counted as helping the next by giving up its place, and its absence is written into the list as a kind of help [C082-P:L8914; C082-P:L8916]. That is an account of moments in strict succession. It is not advice about letting go of things, and this hoe is not a metaphor.

sequence.on_screen: The kiln itself in the last of the daylight: mud and brick, cracked and re-patched, a chimney on one, a thatch roof on another. Smoke leaning one way, then the other. A man moving to the side the wind has chosen for him.
sequence.voice: Another of them is support given simply by being present, by a thing existing while it exists [C082-P:L8230–L8234]. The text's own example for it is the four great elements, holding one another in place, one supporting the other three, three supporting one, two supporting two [C082-P:L8534–L8544]. Nobody here controls the wind. They arrange themselves around it.

sequence.on_screen: A slow tilt from the mouth of the kiln down the outside of the chamber to the tunnel at the base, in one take, with the stone going in at the top and lime coming out at the bottom in the same shot.
sequence.voice: Now the part that this film exists to say. In that summary, two of the six relations have exactly one mode in them. Mind supports matter in one way only, by arising later and holding up what was already there [C083-M:L17; C083-P:L389]. Matter supports mind in one way only, by having been there first [C083-M:L21; C083-P:L393]. Mutual support, where two things hold each other up at once, is one item among nine in the last relation and nowhere else [C083-M:L29]. Most of this runs one way.

sequence.on_screen: Night. The glow at the mouth, the crew working in shifts, stone going in, the hoe going in below. Long, unhurried, the same actions repeating.
sequence.voice: The same summary goes along the chain of dependent arising and counts the conditions at every joint, and the joints are not all the same tightness. Not-knowing is bound into harmful action in seventeen ways and reaches good action in only two [C083-P:L27–L31; C083-P:L33–L67]. Contact supports feeling in eight [C083-P:L287–L305]. Feeling supports wanting in one way only [C083-P:L307], and birth supports ageing and death in one way only [C083-P:L363–L367]. That last line is a count of relations and not a verdict. Ageing and grief are conditioned by having been born. They are not anybody's punishment.

sequence.on_screen: Morning. A draw that has not gone well: hands sorting hot stone on a spread sack, underburnt lumps thrown to one side, fine grey ash to another. Nobody says anything about it.
sequence.voice: The texts have a separate condition for what an intention leaves behind, and they are careful about what its results are like. What ripens is described as inert and quiet, unable to push anything, and it is not handed out as reward or punishment by anyone [C082-P:L6357–L6367; C082-P:L6721]. Nothing this morning has been earned. A load of stone met a fire made of coconut trunk in a week of wind, and this is what came out.

sequence.on_screen: Slaking, at the end of everything: water poured over a heap of quicklime, the heap boiling, steam coming off it in the cold morning, a man turning it with a shovel and standing back. Then, at height again, the smokes and the mountain wall. No commentary over the final minute.
sequence.voice: The summary ends with a line worth hearing exactly. There is no thing at all, past, future or present, inside a person or outside, that is not a condition for something. But only what is itself conditioned can be produced; the unconditioned and mere concepts support without ever being supported [C083-M:L31]. That is not a slogan about connection. It is a map, and the useful questions on it are which way, by what mode, and for how long.

concept_merge.why_together: C083 is the summary and C082 supplies the three conditions this place makes physical. The summary sorts all twenty-four into six relations with fixed counts, six, five, one, one, two and nine [C083-M:L5; C083-P:L369–L417], and it defines the terms of the sort [C083-M:L35]. Two of those relations are the film's argument: mind supports matter in one mode only, by arising afterwards and sustaining what was there already [C083-M:L17; C083-P:L389], and matter supports mind in one mode only, by having arisen first [C083-M:L21; C083-P:L393], while mutuality is one item among the nine of the last relation [C083-M:L29]. The same source then walks the chain of dependent arising and gives the count at each joint, so that not-knowing is shown holding harmful action in seventeen ways and good action in two [C083-P:L27–L31; C083-P:L33–L67], contact holding feeling in eight [C083-P:L287–L305], feeling holding wanting in one [C083-P:L307] and birth holding ageing and death in one [C083-P:L363–L367]; and it closes by saying that nothing whatever fails to be a condition for something, while only what is conditioned can be produced [C083-M:L31]. C082 provides the detail for three of those modes at the scale a camera can see: nutriment, support that has to keep arriving if a continuity is to hold, with the blunt clause that a body deprived of the season's and food's help dies [C082-P:L6843–L6850; C082-P:L6866]; presence, support given by a thing existing while it exists, with the four great elements holding one another as the source's own example [C082-P:L8230–L8234; C082-P:L8534–L8544]; and absence, where a thing's ceasing is itself counted as help because it gives up its place to the next [C082-P:L8914; C082-P:L8916]. A continuously fired lime kiln holds all three at once and holds them in the same frame: fed at the top every hour, standing by being what it is, and unable to take anything new until what is inside has been drawn out of the bottom.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That there is a difference between what started a thing and what is holding it up, and that the difference stops being a nicety when the answer is 'a rag of kerosene four months ago' and 'a basket of stone twenty minutes ago'. It also separates two things a single English word hides, because the kiln cannot receive without also releasing: the drawing at the bottom is not the end of the process but a condition of its continuing, which is what the sources mean when they count a thing's ceasing as a help. And it gives the group the correction it most needs, in footage rather than in a caveat. A kiln has a top and a bottom, and everything in it runs from one to the other. The old version of this idea was a night's firing in a pottery workshop, loaded at dusk and opened when cold, with the tension carried by whether the load survived. It has been moved off that ground for three reasons: a slate that already carries an overnight clamp-kiln film in another group would have had two films watching a fire wait out a night, pottery villages are an archetype the slate has used up, and the old version's real subject was the suspense of a result rather than the anatomy of a support. This kiln never goes out, its charge is stone rather than ware, its product has to be raked out from underneath, and the one dramatic event in it happens only after the fire has finished with the material altogether.

concept_links.why: The digest's six-relation summary is the film's structure and its argument. The counts are narrated as the source gives them [C083-M:L5; C083-P:L369–L417]; the two single-mode relations, later mind sustaining earlier matter and earlier matter supporting later mind, are the fifth beat [C083-M:L17; C083-P:L389; C083-M:L21; C083-P:L393]; mutuality is placed where the source places it, as one of the nine modes of the last relation [C083-M:L29]; and the closing line, that nothing fails to be a condition while only the conditioned can be produced, is the last thing said [C083-M:L31]. The link-by-link counts are used once, in the sixth beat, and are used for their asymmetry [C083-P:L27–L31; C083-P:L33–L67; C083-P:L287–L305; C083-P:L307; C083-P:L363–L367]. Every limit in the digest is honoured and two of them shape the film. 'Everything is mutually interdependent' is refused out loud, because the digest says in as many words that mutuality is only one of the twenty-four and that many relations here run one way only; the fifth beat is that sentence turned into a shot. And the digest's own flag on its editorial reading is respected: the suggestion that the step from feeling to wanting 'leans rather than locks' is marked in the digest as the digest's own inference, going beyond a text that states only the single condition, and needing doctrinal review, so the voice states the count and stops there. The sixth beat also carries the group's hardest correction, that birth conditions ageing and death and that this is not a punishment for anybody, since the source is counting relations. 'Mind over matter' and its opposite are not implied: the single modes are stated as single and limited. 'Positive thinking heals the body' is nowhere in it. Concepts as conditions are mentioned only as part of the count. The digest's uncertainties about a probable print error in the nine modes at rebirth, about the missing target of nutriment-matter [C083-P:L247–L249] and about the garbled line in the summary are not used as material.

Three of the twenty-four, in the digest's own terms, plus one correction. Nutriment is defined as what helps the mind and matter of a being arise again and again, grow in succession and continue unbroken, in four kinds [C082-P:L6843–L6850], with the clause the second beat is built on, that the continuity of kamma-born matter must receive the help of the season and of food and that without it the being dies [C082-P:L6866]. Presence is support given by what has come to be and is standing [C082-P:L8230–L8234], with the four great elements holding one another, one to three, three to one, two to two, as the source's example [C082-P:L8534–L8544]. Absence is the moment that ceases giving its place to the next, counted as a help in its own right and sharing its conditioned states with the proximity condition [C082-P:L8914; C082-P:L8916]. The seventh beat uses the digest's account of results, which it insists are inert and quiet and never a reward or a punishment administered by anyone [C082-P:L6357–L6367; C082-P:L6721], because a draw that comes out underburnt is exactly where a film about conditions could imply desert. The digest's corrections are obeyed. The absence condition is not borrowed as 'letting go makes room for the new', and the third beat says so. Presence is not made into an idea about showing up for people, and the digest's own counter-example, that presence also supports lust when the eye is enjoyed [C082-P:L8712–L8722], is the reason it stays technical. Nutriment is not made into nourishment as a warm idea. The object and decisive-support material, predominance, repetition, the vīthi sequences, the supernormal-knowledge examples and the passages on the gravest acts are unused, and the match-and-box analogy is left to the other films in this group.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the sources distinguish carefully between what brings a thing about and what keeps it going, that the second kind of help has to arrive again and again or the thing stops, and that a thing ceasing is counted as help too, because it gives up its place. And that this is a map with directions on it rather than a claim that everything is connected: most of the support described runs one way, and the counts at each joint of the chain are counts, not judgements on anybody.
what_must_be_real: The kiln's actual continuous burn, on the crew's own rhythm. No kiln is lit, relit, damped, opened or drawn for the camera, and no draw is repeated for a second take. The film works only where the quarry and the kiln are licensed and where the fuel is being obtained lawfully, and it does not follow either question into an accusation. Dust, heat and the load carried are filmed as they are, neither prettified nor turned into an exhibit; nobody is asked to justify their trade, to describe their wages or to say what the work has done to them, and no child at work appears in the film at all. The crew are filmed as people doing skilled work, are not made into characters, and are not asked to confirm any doctrine. Nothing is filmed from a position that puts a crew or a camera near a kiln mouth, a draw tunnel or a slaking heap.
position_hint: late in the group, and a closing candidate: it is the group's summary film, it says the group's correction out loud in footage, and it ends on a change that runs only one way. It should come after the plainer films about what kind of help is meant, because it assumes the viewer already knows the list is a list. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Doubling an existing film. The slate already carries an overnight clamp-kiln film on brick, and any framing that lets this become 'men and a fire at night' loses the one thing that distinguishes it: this fire is never allowed to stop, its charge is stone, and it is emptied from underneath.

Occupational health. Dust in a limestone quarry and heat at a kiln mouth are real harms; filming them beautifully is a way of being on the wrong side, and filming them as an exposé is a different film from this one.
The fuelwood question is live and regulated in this country, and a lingering shot of a coconut-log stack can become an accusation the film has not researched and cannot support.
Letting a bad draw read as desert or as luck. The digest is explicit that results are inert and quiet and not administered by anyone.
Borrowing the absence condition as 'letting go makes room for the new', which is the digest's named misreading.
Making presence into a warm idea about being there for people.
Letting the fire stand in for a life, or the kiln for a body, which is the point at which this group's ethical floor is crossed.
'Everything is connected' as the takeaway, which the fifth beat exists to prevent.
Romanticising hard manual work, or treating a family trade as folklore.
drop_if: No kiln in the district is on a genuinely continuous burn during the window, so the film's central fact would have to be asserted rather than filmed.
The only kilns available are unlicensed, or the quarry supplying them is not, or children are working at either.
The owners will not let a crew stay through the nights, which is when the mouth and the draw are visible at all.
Filming cannot be done without adding to the dust and heat the crew are already working in, or without getting in the way of a draw.
The only way to show a lighting, a dying or a slaking is to have one arranged for the camera.

connections.note: The slate's other kiln film is a clamp of green brick, sealed, burnt for a few nights and taken down once cold, and its subject is not being able to see inside. This one is a permanent pit of stone that is never allowed to go out and is emptied from underneath, and its subject is what has to keep arriving. They should not be scheduled near each other.
Two places kept going by something that has to arrive again within the hour: a town supplied in one direction along a pipe, and a fire fed by hand in alternate layers.
Two films that touch mutual support from opposite sides: one on what holds itself up, this one on where mutuality actually sits in the source's own count, as a single mode among nine.

selection.reason: The place holds both ends of the concept a few metres apart, feeding at the top and drawing at the bottom, and it lets the group's correction about direction be filmed rather than stated.

review.note: Rewritten 2026-09-24 into the footage-led shape, with the firing deliberately moved off the ground the slate has already used. What was dropped: the old subject of a night's wood firing at a pottery workshop, loaded at dusk, fed until dawn, sealed, cooled and opened, with the tension carried by how much of the load survived. Three reasons. The slate already carries an overnight clamp-kiln film in another group, on hand-moulded brick, whose subject is precisely a fire burning through a night inside something nobody can see into, so a second night-firing film would have duplicated it in everything but the ware. Pottery villages are an archetype the slate has exhausted. And the old version's real subject was suspense about a result, which is a different film from an anatomy of support. What replaces it is visibly a different firing: a different material, since the charge is broken limestone and dolomite rather than clay ware; a different kiln, since this is a permanent crucible-shaped pit inside a chamber of mud and brick, with a steel grate and a drawing tunnel, rather than a temporary stack; a different reason, since the object is to turn stone into a powder that reacts with water rather than to harden shaped clay; and a different clock, since the trade here runs kilns on a continuous process that goes on for months and the film's central fact is that the fire is never allowed to go out. The new location's own connection note says this in as many words so the two are not scheduled together. The concepts were kept and re-grounded. C083 is now the six-relation summary and its counts, used for direction and asymmetry, including the two relations that have exactly one mode, and its closing line; the digest's own flag that the 'leans rather than locks' reading of the feeling-to-wanting joint is editorial and needs doctrinal review is respected by stating only the count. C082 now supplies just nutriment, presence and absence, plus the account of results as inert and quiet, which is there to stop a spoiled draw reading as desert. Both digests were re-read from scratch and every citation re-tested against digest evidence; nothing was carried over from the old text.

suggested_location.name: The lime kilns and limestone quarries of the Rattota country, north-east of Matale below the western scarp of the Knuckles

also_known_as.name: Matale aluhunu
also_known_as.meaning: the district's lime, a trade name known nationally for building and agricultural lime
also_known_as.used_by: the trade and the national press

also_known_as.name: hunu
also_known_as.meaning: lime; hunu gal, the stone burnt to make it

also_known_as.name: slaking
also_known_as.meaning: pouring water over burnt quicklime and turning it, which boils and gives off heat, to make the lime usable

suggested_location.region: Matale District, Central Province: the crystalline limestone and dolomite country of the valley and lower slopes north-east of the district town, under the western scarp of the central massif, where quarries and family kilns are spread through farming villages
suggested_location.why_here: Because the concept is the trade's ordinary day here, and because this is the one district where the whole chain sits in one valley: the stone in the ground, the quarry that breaks it by hand, the kiln that burns it, the sorting, the slaking and the bagged lime going out to plasterers and to farmers who need their soil sweetened. The kilns are the right shape for the film, which matters: a crucible pit inside a mud and brick chamber, charged from above in alternate layers of coconut logs and broken stone, grated at the bottom and drawn through a tunnel, so that feeding and emptying are two openings a few metres apart and can be filmed in one move. The trade here runs them continuously rather than in batches, which is the film's central fact and cannot be arranged. The industry is organised, with well over a hundred concerns in the district, most of them small, several thousand people in them and an association of its own, so there is somebody to ask. And the setting gives the aerial the film needs for nothing: a valley of standing white smokes at dawn under a mountain wall.
what_to_film: The valley from height at first light, with the smokes standing up out of the trees under the scarp, and again in low cloud when they lie along it.
A quarry face and the breaking of stone by hand to lumps of an inch or two, in hard light and in dust.
The top of a kiln being charged, in one continuous take: baskets of stone, lengths of coconut trunk laid across, stone again, and the level of the charge sinking between loads.
The bottom of the same kiln: the grate, the long-handled hoe, the tunnel, and hot lime coming out into the shade.
A single slow move from the kiln mouth down the outside of the chamber to the draw tunnel, so that feeding and emptying are in the same shot.
The kiln structure itself held long: patched mud and brick, a twenty-five-foot chimney on one and a coconut-thatch roof on another, smoke leaning with the wind.
The night shift: the glow at the mouth, the crew reading the colour, the same actions repeating with nothing announced.
A draw sorted by hand on a spread sack: good lime, underburnt stone, fine grey ash.
Slaking: water poured on a heap of quicklime, the boiling, the steam in cold morning air, a shovel turning it.
The fuel yard, and the lime going out in bags, filmed plainly and without emphasis.
suggested_location.access: By road north-east from the district town on the mountain road, then on estate and village roads to individual quarries and kilns. Everything depends on the owners, since these are family concerns rather than an institution, and the district association would be the way in. A quarry is a licensed operation under the mines and minerals authority and a kiln near a town is subject to environmental conditions including chimney height, so filming is likely to need the owners' consent and may need the authority's and the local council's as well. Night access to a working kiln is the whole film and is also where the risk is: heat, dust, a draw tunnel and an open mouth, and no protection to speak of. Flying over a valley of working kilns needs the owners' agreement, and the smoke will decide what is possible on any given morning. The dry months are the practical ones; rain stops the quarry.
suggested_location.best_time: The dry months for the quarry, the fuel and a steady burn, with a morning of low cloud sought for the aerial. Within a day, the hour before first light and the hour after dark for the mouth and the draw. Several consecutive days and nights rather than a single visit, because the film's argument is that the same act goes on at every hour, and a second short visit held for a slaking or a relighting, neither of which can be arranged.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only and unverified on the ground. From the sources above: lime has been burnt in this country for a very long time and this district's lime is known nationally by its trade name; the deposits are crystalline limestone and dolomite and are concentrated in the division north-east of the district town; quarries are reported at depths of over fifty feet, with stone broken by sledgehammer for transport and then to a kiln feed of about one to two inches; the traditional kiln is described as a crucible-shaped pit about three to four feet across and five to six feet deep, with a curved bottom, built inside a chamber of mud and brick, with a grating of steel rod at the base to hold back unburnt material and a tunnel through which the burnt lime is removed; it is charged with alternate layers of heavy timber, two to three feet long and four to twelve inches thick, and stone, at roughly eight to ten cubic yards of firewood to fifty cubic feet of aggregate, and lit with kerosene-soaked rags; the burn is described as passing about 480 degrees for the magnesium carbonate and about 900 for the calcium carbonate, running continuously for days with more material added as the level drops, and the district's trade is reported to run kilns on a continuous process that can go on for up to a year; lime is tapped through the grating with long-handled hoes and drawn out through the tunnel, then sorted by hand from underburnt stone and from ash, which is distinguished by its fineness and colour; slaking is done by pouring water over a large pile of quicklime and mixing it by shovel, with a good deal of air slaking before that; fuel is coconut trunk and husk, which is noted as heating unevenly, and fuelwood supply has been constrained by transport rules; kilns near populated areas are required to carry chimneys up to twenty-five feet while rural ones have only a coconut-thatch roof over the mouth; and the district is reported to hold 177 lime concerns, more than half of them small, employing on the order of three thousand people, with an association formed about a decade ago to protect small producers from middlemen. The coordinates point at the small town at the centre of that country and are not a survey: no quarry, kiln, owner or village has been identified. Three things the film depends on are inferences rather than confirmed facts about any particular kiln: that a continuously fired kiln can be found and filmed through its nights, that the crew read the burn by the colour at the mouth and by the wind rather than by instruments, and that a slaking can be reached inside the window. Nobody has been approached and no permission has been sought from any owner, from the association or from the minerals or environmental authorities. No photograph of a lime kiln, a quarry or the lime country was found on Wikimedia Commons; both images are of the surrounding hill country and the mountain wall above it.

unknowns: Whether kilns here are in fact run continuously for months at a time, which is the film's central claim, and whether one on a long burn can be found in the window.
Whether owners will let a crew stay through the nights, which is the only time the mouth and the draw can be filmed.
Who else must agree: the minerals authority for the quarry, the local council and the environmental authority for the kiln, and the district association as the way in.
Whether the burn is judged by eye and wind as the film assumes, or by something else entirely.
Whether a slaking, a relighting or a kiln allowed to die can be reached at all inside a filming window, since none of them can be arranged.
Whether the work can be filmed without adding to the dust and heat the crew are already in, and whether a crew can be kept clear of a draw.
Whether the licensing of the quarries and the lawfulness of the fuel supply can be established well enough to film without either ignoring the question or making an accusation.
